title: Phase-Drift Limits and Adaptive Quadrature Readout in Programmable Photonic Processors
authors: Gökhan Elmas, Igor A. Litvin, Janis Nötzel
abstract: Phase fluctuations between optical inputs limit programmable photonic processors because their output powers depend on coherent interference. We study the phase-drift penalty that arises when sine and cosine quadratures are measured sequentially rather than simultaneously. The analysis is motivated by measurements from an eight-mode programmable photonic processor, including 35 free-running recordings of 300 s acquired at approximately 125 samples per second per channel. These recordings provide an empirical route for estimating the phase-increment variance at a selected reconfiguration interval.   The estimate is defined at the time of the second measurement. For fixed quadrature order, perturbation of the atan2 reconstruction gives $e_{C\to S}=-δ_τ\sin^2φ_0+O(δ_τ^2)$ and $e_{S\to C}=-δ_τ\cos^2φ_0+O(δ_τ^2)$. Writing $Q_τ=\operatorname{Var}(δ_τ)$, uniform phase averaging gives the first-order drift mean-square error $3Q_τ/8$. A phase-predicted ordering rule measures the locally less informative quadrature first and the more informative quadrature second. Its uniform first-order penalty is $(3/8-1/π)Q_τ$, which is 84.9 percent below the fixed-order value.   We also derive an increment-aware estimator from a local state-space model. Marginalizing the unknown phase increment increases the variance of a stale phase observation by $Q_τ$, reducing its Fisher information from $I$ to $I/(1+IQ_τ)$. For ideal balanced Poisson detection, the Fisher information of each quadrature equals its detected signal-photon number. This yields dimensionless architecture boundaries in spatial information and phase-increment variance. Nonlinear Monte Carlo simulations validate the perturbative laws, quantify robustness to prediction error, and compare simultaneous, fixed-order, increment-aware, and adaptive receivers under a common noise model.
summary: This paper analyzes the fundamental limits on phase estimation in programmable photonic processors when measuring quadrature components sequentially. It develops a theory showing that adaptive measurement ordering can drastically reduce errors caused by unknown phase drift compared to fixed protocols. The results provide crucial guidelines for designing robust quantum optical hardware.
main_problem: The research quantifies the phase-drift penalty incurred when sequentially measuring sine and cosine quadratures in programmable photonic processors, compared to simultaneous measurement.
main_result: An adaptive ordering rule significantly outperforms fixed-order methods, reducing the drift-induced Mean Square Error by up to 84.9%.
method: The authors derive theoretical bounds using Fisher information and analyze estimation errors based on small-angle approximations for $	ext{atan2}$ reconstruction.
model_or_system: The study uses an eight-mode programmable photonic processor that converts relative optical phases into measurable sine and cosine power pairs, simulating phase evolution over time intervals ($	au$).
key_observables: Phase-drift penalty (MSE), Fisher Information ($I_{sp}, I_t$), and the effective information gain factor ($g$).
important_parameters: The phase-increment variance ($Q_	au$) is critical, as are dimensionless products like $I_{sp}Q_	au$ which define operational regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on first-order approximations for error terms and assumes ideal balanced Poisson detection statistics for the Fisher information derivation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the eight-mode processor setup, quadrature extraction, and compare receiver performance (e.g., Figure 7) across different estimation strategies under a common noise model.
paper_structure: The paper moves from defining the physical measurement problem (quadrature readout) to deriving error bounds for fixed vs. adaptive temporal measurements, culminating in an information-theoretic comparison of various estimators.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses resource limitations and estimation fidelity in photonic quantum computation platforms by providing rigorous theoretical limits on phase estimation accuracy under realistic noise models.
